claim: For covariate shift, the sources describe weighted conformal prediction as relying on a likelihood ratio between training and test covariate distributions.
quote: Specifically, they propose weighted conformal prediction (WCP) to deal with covariate shifts where the likelihood ratio between the training P X and test PX covariate distributions is known.

claim: Another source states the assumptions more sharply: the conditional distribution of Y given X must stay constant, and the likelihood ratio must be known or very accurately estimated.
quote: However, this requires the conditional distribution of Y |X to be constant between training and testing and the likelihood ratio P 1 (X)/P 0 (X) to be either known or very accurately estimated.

claim: The DriftGuard paper says importance weighting can restore validity under covariate shift when density ratios are known.
quote: Importance weighting can restore validity under covariate shift when density ratios are known.

claim: The same paper reports that, under unrestricted conditional shift, the identified set for target coverage is the whole interval [0,1].
quote: We establish exact and approximate detectability bounds, a minimax testing consequence, and a sharp $[0,1]$ identified set for target coverage under unrestricted conditional shift.

claim: One covariate-shift paper claims near-optimal conditional coverage by adaptive prediction sets whenever the likelihood ratio is estimable at a sufficient rate.
quote: paired with adaptive prediction sets (APS) that achieve near-optimal conditional coverage rates whenever the likelihood ratio is estimable at a sufficient rate (Theorem 4.3).

claim: A further source gives a finite-sample guarantee for weighted conformal procedures only under bounded density ratios.
quote: Third, under covariate shift with bounded density ratios, a weighted conformal procedure restores finite-sample coverage guarantees, with an explicit error bound when the density ratio is estimated via epistemic uncertainty (Theorem 3).

claim: For label shift, the evidence is thin. One source shows that label-weighted conformal prediction can give a finite-sample macro-coverage guarantee.
quote: In this work, we show that label-weighted conformal prediction can be used to produce prediction sets with a finite-sample macro-coverage guarantee

claim: One analysis of pseudo-calibration under a bounded label-conditional covariate shift model derives a lower bound on target coverage in terms of the source-domain loss of the classifier and a Wasserstein measure of the shift.
quote: Using tools from domain adaptation, we derive a lower bound on target coverage in terms of the source-domain loss of the classifier and a Wasserstein measure of the shift.

claim: For temporal drift, adaptive conformal inference is reported to achieve the desired coverage frequency over long time intervals irrespective of the true data generating process.
quote: our adaptive approach provably achieves the desired coverage frequency over long-time intervals irrespective of the true data generating process.

claim: For adaptive conformal inference, the unconditional guarantee concerns long-run coverage; the authors also show that when the distribution shift is small and the prediction algorithm takes a certain simple form, ACI additionally obtains approximate marginal coverage at most time steps.
quote: Moreover, when the distribution shift is small and the prediction algorithm takes a certain simple form we show that ACI will additionally obtain approximate marginal coverage at most time steps.

claim: Conformal PID control states that its quantile tracking achieves long-run coverage under no assumptions except boundedness of the scores.
quote: Running online gradient descent on the quantile loss (summed over all past scores) gives rise to a method that we call quantile tracking, which achieves long-run coverage (2) under no assumptions except boundedness of the scores.
locator: sec. Peek at results: methods, para 7

claim: The strongly adaptive variant is said to achieve provably small regret over all local time intervals of a given width.
quote: develop a novel procedure with provably small regret over all local time intervals of a given width.

claim: A heuristic ensemble method is explicitly said to offer no analogous regret or coverage guarantee.
quote: PACE is heuristic and does not provide an analogous regret or coverage guarantee.

claim: For non-exchangeable calibration with weights, the introductory review says weighted procedures for drift always satisfy marginal coverage and are exact when the magnitude of the shift is known.
quote: The following theory provides some justification for such weighted conformal procedures; in particular, they always satisfy marginal coverage, and are exact when the magnitude of the distribution shift is known.
locator: sec. Conformal Prediction Under Distribution Drift, para 143

claim: The same review notes that, in a weather example, total-variation distance between adjacent points could not be measured, so no formal coverage bound was available.
quote: There is no hope of measuring the TV distance between adjacent data points in order to apply Theorem 4, so we cannot get a formal coverage bound.
locator: sec. Weather Prediction with Time-Series Distribution Shift, para 162

claim: The time-series EnbPI method gives coverage-gap bounds that converge to zero only under additional assumptions.
quote: Theoretically, we establish explicit bounds on conditional and marginal coverage gaps of estimated prediction intervals, which asymptotically converge to zero under additional assumptions.

claim: A temporal knowledge-graph study ties a conditional coverage gap to local volatility under bounded local exchangeability.
quote: We provide a theoretical footing by proving a per-slice Mondrian bound under bounded local exchangeability, which ties the conditional coverage gap to local temporal-edge volatility.

claim: An applied study of lab-to-track thermal transfer reports that density-ratio weighting of EnbPI gave only a modest improvement in coverage, which the authors describe as not a complete fix.
quote: This recovers coverage to 72.42%, a modest, honestly-reported improvement, not a complete fix.
